newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraq still wielding oil as political weapon.
newsitem.headline: Iraq still wielding oil as political weapon.

text.p: Iraq, strangled by six years of sanctions, is winning political support in the United Nations Security Council by offering a keenly sought prize -- production rights in some of the world's most prolific oilfields.
Security Council permanent members China, Russia and France are moving to take a post-sanctions stake in Iraq's oilfields, rivalled in size only by those in Saudi Arabia.

"The oil offer is the leading cog in Baghdad's plan to get the sanctions completely lifted and to get some sort of economic normality in place...Oil is its leading and probably only decent card," one Western analyst based in the Gulf said.

Iraq's proven oil reserves officially stand at more than 112 billion barrels, some 11 percent of the world's total reserves, although its potential has been drastically held back because of its 1980-1988 war with Iran and the 1991 Gulf War.
China on Monday showed it was ready to restore Iraq's war and sanctions battered petroleum industry, saying it was in talks with Iraq on signing huge oil exploration contracts.
The official Xinhua news agency said the two sides were discussing a plan for China to help Iraq develop its oilfields.

Iraqi authorities last month initialled the first oilfield contract since 1990 with the China National Petroleum Corporation to develop Iraq's Al-Ahdab field, according to the Middle East Economic Survey (MEES) newsletter.

Further evidence of future possible foreign oil involvement in Iraq was seen over the weekend when Iraq's official media reported visits to Baghdad by representatives of France's Elf Aquitaine and Total SA.

Any oil deal can be carried out only when U.N. sanctions are lifted. The sanctions bind Baghdad to observe all Gulf War ceasefire terms, including the complete accounting for and destruction of its weapons of mass destruction.
Even a limited oil-for-food deal struck with the U.N. has stalled after Kurdish infighting in northern Iraq resulted in U.S. cruise missile attacks in southern Iraq in September.
"No one expects Iraqi oil this year...it's a forgotten factor in this market," an oil trader based in the United Arab Emirates said.
But despite Iraq's lack of progress in lifting U.N. sanctions, the oil prize is still earning Iraqi President Saddam Hussein some political leverage out of complete isolation.

Beijing, Moscow and Paris have consistently pressed for Iraq to be allowed to export a limited amount of oil for aid purposes and have also been regular critics of U.S. policy and military action against Baghdad.

China in September criticised the no-fly zones imposed over Iraq by Gulf War allies as a violation of Iraqi sovereignty while Paris has highlighted the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Iraq to kick-start the oil-for-food deal.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, after meeting Iraqi deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz in Moscow on Sunday, called for the Security Council to allow Iraq to export oil under a U.N. deal struck in May that would let Baghdad export $2 billion of its oil every six months for humanitarian supplies.

Moscow, trying to recoup a $7 billion debt from Baghdad, has signed an agreement covering oil exploration and refining and has said it wanted to set up a joint venture company to explore for oil in Iraq.
